François Quesnay. An eighteenth century French physician and economist who founded the Physiocratic school of thought, though his ideas were later eclipsed by Adam Smith and David Ricardo.

The Physiocrats believed something radical for their time: that agriculture is the sole source of economic value. Manufacturing merely transforms existing materials and adds no net value. Only the land produces a genuine surplus beyond the cost of inputs. This focus on agriculture made sense in a largely rural, pre-industrial world, but it would prove a dead end as industrialization advanced.

Quesnay created the Tableau Économique, or Economic Table, an early input-output model showing how economic surplus flows between landowners, farmers, and artisans. It was a pioneering attempt to model the whole economy systematically.

He argued that only land-based output generates true wealth. Government revenue should therefore come from a single tax on land, since all other income ultimately derives from land value. This was the birth of the single-tax idea. He opposed the feudal restrictions that prevented grain from moving freely between regions, arguing instead for freer commerce. This aligned with the broader Enlightenment push for economic reform.

Quesnay held significant influence. He served as physician to King Louis XV and had access to French royal circles. Though his specific economic theories about agriculture as the sole source of value were eventually abandoned, his systematic approach to modeling the economy as an interconnected whole influenced later thinkers. Adam Smith admired Quesnay's systematic approach, though Smith rejected the exclusive focus on agriculture and incorporated Physiocratic ideas selectively into The Wealth of Nations. David Ricardo later refashioned Quesnay's rent theory into a more general framework that worked for industrial economies. Even Karl Marx's later theory owed a debt to Physiocratic analysis of production and surplus.
